q: Waves are classified as progressive waves and ____.
e: Waves are broadly classified into progressive waves, which spread out, and stationary waves, which remain in the region they are produced.

q: Progressive waves spread out from the ____ in which they are produced.
e: Progressive waves travel outward from their source region, carrying energy through the medium.

q: Unlike progressive waves, stationary waves do not spread out but remain in the ____ in which they are produced.
e: Stationary waves are confined to the region of their production, which is why they are also called standing waves.

q: So stationary waves are also called ____ waves.
e: Because they do not spread out, stationary waves are alternatively referred to as standing waves.

q: Progressive waves carry ____ through the medium.
e: A defining characteristic of progressive waves is their ability to transport energy from one point to another through the medium.

q: A stationary wave is the resultant wave by the ____ of two waves of the same type having equal amplitudes and velocities traveling in opposite directions.
e: Stationary waves are formed through the principle of superposition when two identical waves travel in opposite directions.

q: When two or more waves pass the same point the resultant wave at that point is the ____ of the individual waves.
e: The principle of superposition states that the resultant displacement is the algebraic sum of the individual wave displacements.

q: This is called principle of ____.
e: The rule that the resultant wave is the sum of individual waves passing the same point is known as the principle of superposition.

q: If the resultant wave has a larger amplitude than that of individual waves, this is said to be ____ interference.
e: Constructive interference occurs when waves combine to produce a resultant wave with a larger amplitude.

q: If the resultant wave has a smaller amplitude than that of individual waves, this is said to be ____ interference.
e: Destructive interference occurs when waves combine to produce a resultant wave with a smaller amplitude.

q: One characteristic of every stationary wave pattern is that there are points along the medium, which are called ____ and antinodes.
e: Stationary wave patterns are characterized by alternating points of zero displacement (nodes) and maximum displacement (antinodes).

q: The points that are always stationary in a stationary wave pattern are called ____.
e: Nodes are the specific points along the medium in a stationary wave that remain completely stationary.

q: The mid-points between successive nodes have the largest amplitudes and are called ____.
e: Antinodes are located exactly halfway between successive nodes and experience the maximum amplitude of vibration.

q: Nodes and antinodes always ____ and are equally spaced.
e: In a stationary wave pattern, nodes and antinodes strictly alternate with equal spacing between them.

q: The distance between two successive nodes (or) antinodes is equal to ____.
e: The spatial distance between any two consecutive nodes or any two consecutive antinodes is exactly half the wavelength.

q: The distance from a node to the nearest antinode is equal to ____.
e: Since nodes and antinodes alternate and are spaced by $\lambda/2$, the distance from a node to the adjacent antinode is a quarter of the wavelength.

q: In most musical instruments, the stretched ____ act as a source of sound.
e: String instruments like violins and mandolins produce sound through the vibration of stretched strings.

q: When the stretched strings are plucked, the ____ waves are produced.
e: Plucking a stretched string fixed at both ends generates stationary waves due to the reflection of waves at the fixed ends.

q: The waves that are formed on a vibrating string are called ____.
e: The specific standing wave patterns with nodes at the fixed ends of a vibrating string are referred to as harmonics.

q: For the $n^{th}$ harmonic, the wavelength is given by the formula ____.
e: The wavelength of the $n^{th}$ harmonic on a string of length $l$ is determined by dividing twice the length by the harmonic number $n$.

q: The corresponding frequencies are calculated from ____, where $v$ is the velocity of wave in a string.
e: The wave equation $v = f_n \lambda_n$ relates the wave velocity, frequency, and wavelength for any harmonic.

q: The frequencies of a vibrating string of length $l$ are given by ____.
e: By substituting the wavelength formula into the wave equation, the frequency of the $n^{th}$ harmonic is found to be $nv/2l$.

q: Vibration of a string in one single segment is called the ____ or first harmonic.
e: The lowest frequency of vibration, where the string vibrates in a single segment, is known as the fundamental frequency.

q: A musical tone which is part of the harmonic series above a fundamental note is called an ____.
e: Overtones are the higher-frequency tones in the harmonic series that occur above the fundamental frequency.

q: The velocity of a wave in a vibrating string depends on the tension of the string and mass per unit length of the string as follows: ____.
e: Wave velocity in a string is directly proportional to the square root of tension and inversely proportional to the square root of mass per unit length.

q: In the wave velocity formula for a string, $T$ represents the ____ of the string.
e: In the formula $v = \sqrt{T/\mu}$, the variable $T$ denotes the tension applied to the string.

q: Mass per unit length of the string, denoted by $\mu$, is the ratio of ____ to length of the string.
e: The linear mass density $\mu$ is calculated by dividing the total mass of the string by its total length.

q: The mass of the string can be expressed as $m = \rho V =$ ____.
e: By substituting volume $V$ with the product of cross-sectional area $A$ and length $l$, mass can be written as $\rho A l$.

q: In the mass formula for a string, $\rho$ represents the ____ of the material of the string.
e: The symbol $\rho$ stands for the density of the material from which the string is made.

q: Pendulum C will oscillate with the greatest amplitude since its ____ matches that of pendulum A which provides the driving force.
e: Maximum amplitude oscillation occurs when the driven system's natural frequency matches the frequency of the driving force.

q: The amplitude of the motion reaches a maximum when the frequency of driving force equals the ____ of the system.
e: Resonance is the condition where the driving frequency equals the system's natural frequency, resulting in maximum amplitude.

q: Under this condition, the system is said to be in ____.
e: When the driving frequency matches the natural frequency, the phenomenon is called resonance.

q: The frequency at which resonance occurs is called the ____ of the system.
e: The specific frequency that causes a system to resonate is known as its resonant frequency.

q: Natural frequency is the frequency at which a system tends to oscillate in the absence of any ____.
e: Natural frequency is an intrinsic property of a system, observed when it oscillates freely without external driving forces.

q: The resonant sound will be heard at certain different length of ____.
e: In a resonance column experiment, resonance is achieved at specific lengths of the air column above the water.

q: A resonance column tube will have an ____ near the open end and a node at the water surface.
e: At the open end of a resonance tube, air molecules can move freely, forming an antinode.

q: At the closed end of a resonance column, a ____ will be formed because air molecules cannot move.
e: The water surface acts as a closed end, preventing air molecule movement and thus forming a node.

q: Resonance can only be produced under the situation where a node is formed at the water surface and an ____ is formed at the open end.
e: The boundary conditions for resonance in a closed tube require a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end.

q: Using the resonance equations, the wavelength of the vibrating air column is ____.
e: By taking the difference between the second and first resonance lengths, the end correction is eliminated, yielding $\lambda = 2(l_2 - l_1)$.

q: At resonance, the velocity of sound can be found using the formula ____.
e: Once the wavelength is determined from resonance lengths, the speed of sound is calculated by multiplying it by the known frequency of the tuning fork.

q: In closed organ pipes, an antinode exists near the open end while a ____ is formed at the closed end.
e: Closed organ pipes have a node at the closed end and an antinode near the open blowing end.

q: The wavelength of the $n^{th}$ harmonic for a vibrating air column in a closed organ pipe is ____.
e: For a closed organ pipe, the wavelength of the $n^{th}$ harmonic is four times the length of the pipe divided by the odd harmonic number $n$.

q: The frequency of a closed organ pipe is given by the formula ____.
e: The resonant frequencies of a closed organ pipe are odd multiples of the fundamental frequency, given by $nv/4l$.

q: A closed organ pipe produces only ____ harmonics.
e: Due to the boundary conditions of a node at one end and an antinode at the other, closed organ pipes can only produce odd harmonics.

q: In a closed organ pipe, the third harmonic is called the first ____.
e: Since closed pipes only produce odd harmonics, the next possible frequency after the fundamental is the third harmonic, which is the first overtone.

q: The stationary wave with a single node in the open organ pipe corresponds to ____ (first harmonic).
e: In an open organ pipe, the simplest standing wave pattern with a single node in the middle represents the fundamental frequency.

q: The wavelength for the $n^{th}$ harmonic in an open organ pipe is ____.
e: For an open organ pipe, the wavelength of the $n^{th}$ harmonic is twice the length of the pipe divided by the harmonic number $n$.

q: The frequencies of a vibrating air column in an open organ pipe are given by ____.
e: Open organ pipes produce all integer harmonics, with frequencies calculated as $nv/2l$.

q: A flute can be modeled as a pipe open at both ends, while a clarinet can be modeled as a pipe ____ at one end.
e: Flutes act as open organ pipes, whereas clarinets function as closed organ pipes due to the mouthpiece closing one end.

q: Beats are the periodic fluctuation heard in the ____ of sound when two sound waves of slightly different frequencies interfere with one another.
e: Beats manifest as a pulsating variation in loudness or intensity due to the alternating constructive and destructive interference of two close frequencies.

q: The number of beats per second, or beat frequency, is the ____ in frequency between the two sources.
e: The beat frequency is exactly equal to the absolute difference between the frequencies of the two interfering sound waves.

q: The beat frequency is calculated using the formula ____.
e: The formula for beat frequency is the absolute value of the difference between the two source frequencies, $f_1$ and $f_2$.

q: The intensity of a wave is the power or energy per unit time transported per unit ____.
e: Wave intensity is defined as the rate of energy flow per unit area perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation.

q: The intensity of a wave is calculated using the formula ____.
e: Intensity $I$ is the ratio of the wave's power $P$ to the cross-sectional area $A$ over which it is distributed.

q: In the intensity formula, $P$ represents the ____ of the wave.
e: In the equation $I = P/A$, the variable $P$ stands for the power, or energy per unit time, of the wave.

q: In SI units, the unit of intensity of a wave is ____.
e: The standard SI unit for wave intensity is watts per square metre ($W m^{-2}$).

q: By considering the source of sound as a point source, the sound wave can be distributed uniformly over a spherical wave front of area ____.
e: Sound from a point source spreads out spherically, so the area over which the power is distributed is the surface area of a sphere, $4\pi r^2$.

q: Hence, the wave intensity at a distance $r$ from a point source is ____.
e: Substituting the spherical area into the intensity formula gives $I = P / (4\pi r^2)$ for a point source.

q: For a particular source, intensity varies ____ with the square of the distance from the source.
e: As the distance from the source increases, the intensity decreases proportionally to the square of that distance.

q: Intensity of a wave obeys the ____ law.
e: The relationship where intensity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance is known as the inverse square law.

q: The intensity of a wave is directly proportional to the ____ of the amplitude of the wave.
e: A fundamental property of waves is that their intensity is directly proportional to the square of their amplitude.
